title: Physical Science — Structure of Matter
description: Study atomic structure, the periodic table, and chemical bonding.
objectives: Describe atomic models historically and currently
Read the periodic table (periods, groups, blocks)
Explain ionic and covalent bonding

lessons.title: Modern Atomic Model
lessons.content: The modern quantum model describes electrons in probability clouds called orbitals.
examples: Bohr model (1913): electrons in fixed orbits — useful but simplified
Electron cloud model: electrons exist in regions of probability
Electron configuration determines chemical behavior

lessons.title: Chemical Bonding
lessons.content: Atoms bond to achieve stable electron configurations.
examples: Ionic bond: electron transfer between metal and non-metal (NaCl: Na⁺ and Cl⁻)
Covalent bond: electron sharing between non-metals (H₂O: O shares electrons with 2 H)
Metallic bond: sea of electrons shared among metal atoms → conducts electricity

title: Acids, Bases, and pH
description: Understand acid-base chemistry and the pH scale.
objectives: Define acids and bases in terms of H⁺ ions
Read and use the pH scale
Describe neutralization reactions

lessons.title: Acids and Bases
lessons.content: Acids release H⁺ ions; bases accept H⁺ (or release OH⁻).
examples: Acids: lemon juice, vinegar, stomach acid (HCl)
Bases: baking soda, soap, bleach
Strong acid: HCl completely dissociates; weak acid: acetic acid partially dissociates

lessons.title: pH Scale
lessons.content: pH measures hydrogen ion concentration on a scale of 0-14.
examples: pH < 7: acidic; pH = 7: neutral; pH > 7: basic
Battery acid: pH ~1; pure water: pH 7; bleach: pH ~13
Neutralization: acid + base → salt + water

title: Motion and Forces — Advanced
description: Deepen understanding of kinematics and dynamics.
objectives: Analyze motion with graphs
Apply Newton's laws to complex systems
Understand momentum and impulse

lessons.title: Kinematics
lessons.content: Kinematics describes motion without considering its cause.
examples: Displacement-time graph: slope = velocity
Velocity-time graph: slope = acceleration; area = displacement
Uniform acceleration: v = u + at; s = ut + ½at²

lessons.title: Dynamics
lessons.content: Newton's laws applied to complex systems.
examples: Free body diagram: draw all forces on an object
Atwood machine: two masses over a pulley — net force = (m₁−m₂)g
Projectile motion: horizontal (constant velocity) + vertical (acceleration due to gravity)

title: Energy — Heat and Thermodynamics
description: Study heat transfer, thermal energy, and the laws of thermodynamics.
objectives: Distinguish temperature from thermal energy
Describe heat transfer mechanisms
Apply the first and second laws of thermodynamics

lessons.title: Heat Transfer
lessons.content: Thermal energy moves from hot to cold by three mechanisms.
examples: Conduction: direct contact (metal spoon in hot soup)
Convection: fluid movement (hot air rises, cool air sinks)
Radiation: electromagnetic waves (sun heats Earth across vacuum)

lessons.title: Laws of Thermodynamics
lessons.content: Energy is conserved; entropy always increases.
examples: 1st Law: energy cannot be created or destroyed; ΔU = Q − W
2nd Law: heat flows naturally from hot to cold; disorder (entropy) increases
Why machines can't be 100% efficient: some energy always lost to heat

title: Electromagnetism
description: Explore the relationship between electricity and magnetism.
objectives: Describe magnetic fields and poles
Explain electromagnetic induction
Understand how motors and generators work

lessons.title: Magnetic Fields
lessons.content: Every magnet creates a magnetic field; electric currents also create magnetic fields.
examples: Earth acts like a giant magnet — magnetic north is near geographic north
Oersted (1820): discovered that current-carrying wire deflects a compass
Solenoid: coil of wire carrying current creates a strong magnetic field (electromagnet)

lessons.title: Induction and Devices
lessons.content: A changing magnetic field induces an electric current.
examples: Faraday's Law of Induction (1831): moving a magnet through a coil generates electricity
Generator: converts mechanical energy to electrical energy (rotating magnet in coil)
Motor: converts electrical energy to mechanical (current in magnetic field creates force)

title: Geology — Earth's History
description: Read the rock record, understand geological processes, and Earth's changing surface.
objectives: Apply principles of stratigraphy
Explain geological processes: weathering, erosion, deposition
Describe major geological eras and events

lessons.title: Rock Types and Cycles
lessons.content: Rocks form through igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic processes in a continuous cycle.
examples: Igneous: cooled magma/lava (granite, basalt)
Sedimentary: compacted sediment (sandstone, limestone) — contains fossils
Metamorphic: transformed by heat/pressure (marble from limestone, quartzite from sandstone)

lessons.title: Geological Time
lessons.content: Earth's 4.6-billion-year history is divided into eons, eras, periods, and epochs.
examples: Precambrian: 88% of Earth's history; single-celled life
Paleozoic: Cambrian explosion, first vertebrates, mass extinctions
Mesozoic: age of dinosaurs; ~66 Ma ended by asteroid impact
Cenozoic: mammals dominate; last 65.5 million years; humans appear in last 0.3 Ma

title: Ecology — Population Dynamics
description: Analyze how populations change over time and interact within ecosystems.
objectives: Describe factors that limit population growth
Explain predator-prey dynamics
Analyze human population growth and its implications

lessons.title: Population Growth Models
lessons.content: Populations grow exponentially when unlimited but logistically when resources are limited.
examples: J-curve: exponential growth (no resource limits) — bacteria in ideal conditions
S-curve: logistic growth (real-world carrying capacity)
Carrying capacity (K): maximum population an environment can support

lessons.title: Limiting Factors
lessons.content: Biotic and abiotic factors limit population size.
examples: Density-dependent: disease, competition, predation — effects increase with population density
Density-independent: natural disasters, extreme weather — affect populations regardless of size
Predator-prey oscillations: Lotka-Volterra model; lynx-hare cycles

title: Nuclear Physics — Introduction
description: Introduce nuclear reactions, radioactivity, and nuclear energy.
objectives: Describe types of radioactive decay
Explain fission and fusion
Evaluate nuclear energy's role in the future

lessons.title: Radioactive Decay
lessons.content: Unstable nuclei release radiation to become more stable.
examples: Alpha decay: releases α particle (2p + 2n) — least penetrating
Beta decay: releases β particle (electron) — from neutron → proton
Gamma decay: releases high-energy photon — most penetrating

lessons.title: Fission and Fusion
lessons.content: Both nuclear reactions release enormous energy via E = mc².
examples: Fission: heavy nucleus splits (U-235 + neutron → two smaller nuclei + energy) — used in nuclear power plants and bombs
Fusion: two light nuclei combine (H + H → He + energy) — powers the sun; experimental fusion reactors (ITER) aim for commercial power by 2040s
Fusion produces ~4× more energy than fission per kg; no long-lived radioactive waste

title: Biomedical Science
description: Explore how biology and medicine intersect through disease, immunity, and modern treatments.
objectives: Describe how the immune system works
Explain how vaccines work
Analyze modern medical technologies

lessons.title: The Immune System
lessons.content: The immune system defends the body through innate and adaptive immunity.
examples: Innate: skin, fever, inflammation — first line of defense (non-specific)
Adaptive: B-cells (antibodies) and T-cells (kill infected cells) — specific response, develops memory
Autoimmune disorders: immune system attacks own cells (lupus, MS, type 1 diabetes)

lessons.title: Vaccines and Modern Medicine
lessons.content: Vaccines train the immune system; modern medicine has revolutionized health.
examples: Vaccines: introduce antigen (weakened pathogen or mRNA) → immune memory formed → fast response if exposed to real pathogen
mRNA vaccines (COVID-19): instruct cells to make spike protein — new platform for many diseases
Antibiotics: kill bacteria by disrupting cell walls or protein synthesis; antibiotic resistance is a growing crisis

title: Physics — Waves and Modern Technology
description: Explore wave behavior and how wave physics underpins modern technology.
objectives: Describe wave behaviors: reflection, refraction, diffraction, interference
Explain how digital technology uses waves
Connect wave physics to medical and communication technology

lessons.title: Wave Behaviors
lessons.content: Waves interact with matter and each other in predictable ways.
examples: Reflection: waves bounce off surfaces (mirrors, echo)
Refraction: waves bend when entering a new medium (lens, prism)
Diffraction: waves bend around obstacles (sound around corners)
Interference: waves add (constructive) or cancel (destructive)

lessons.title: Wave Technology
lessons.content: Wave physics underlies nearly all modern communication and medical technology.
examples: MRI: uses radio waves and magnetic fields to image soft tissue
Ultrasound: high-frequency sound waves create images of internal organs (pregnancy imaging, heart scans)
Fiber optics: total internal reflection carries data as light pulses at the speed of light
Wi-Fi and 5G: radio waves carry digital data; different frequencies for different uses
